content.text: A clustering algorithm always returns groups, even from data that has none, and the groups follow the algorithm's own definition of a cluster. k-means assumes compact, round groups of similar spread. Decide what a group means for your problem, choose a method that shares that definition, and check the result against evidence from outside the clustering.

A marketing team runs k-means on two scaled columns, monthly spend and visit frequency. They try k from 2 to 6 and keep k=4, because it has the best silhouette score: 0.413. Four personas get names, photos and a slide deck. But the data in the first script below is uniform noise: customers spread evenly, with no groups at all. k-means didn't discover four segments. It cut a square into four pieces, the way it would cut anything.
The common misconception
"Clustering reveals the natural, true groups that exist in the data." It's an easy belief to hold:

items.text: It's called unsupervised learning, which sounds like the algorithm finds structure with no human assumptions.
The output looks authoritative: every row gets a label, every group gets a center, and a metric gives a number.
On textbook demos with well-separated round blobs,
really does recover the groups that generated the data, exactly.

content.text: The half-truth: when groups are compact, round, similar in spread and well apart, k-means finds them. But that's the data agreeing with an assumption the algorithm made in advance. Change the data, and the same algorithm still answers, just as confidently.
What actually happens

A clustering algorithm doesn't look for groups in general. It optimizes one specific definition of a group, and it returns the best answer under that definition, whether or not the data has that shape.
Every algorithm brings its own definition of a group

k-means places k centers to minimize inertia, the sum of squared distances from each point to its nearest center. scikit-learn's guide spells out the price: inertia assumes clusters are convex and isotropic, so k-means "responds poorly to elongated clusters, or manifolds with irregular shapes." Its k-means assumptions example adds that k-means behaves like a mixture of Gaussians that all share the same variance, so groups with very different spreads also break it.

Other methods define a group differently. DBSCAN treats clusters as areas of high density separated by areas of low density, so they can take any shape. A Gaussian mixture fits ellipses, each with its own shape and spread. Agglomerative clustering depends on the linkage you choose. None of these definitions is the true one; each fits some data and not other data.
It always returns k groups

For k-means, k is an input, not a finding: Google's clustering course lists "k must be chosen manually" as its first disadvantage. scikit-learn's assumptions example goes further: in a real setting there is no uniquely defined true number of clusters, and the right number has to come from data-based criteria and knowledge of the intended goal. Its algorithm-comparison example even includes a "null" dataset, homogeneous data with no good clustering. Given a k, k-means splits it anyway, as the first script shows.
Scores share the algorithm's assumptions
Without known labels, people judge clusters with internal scores such as the
silhouette coefficient

. For each point it compares a, the mean distance to its own cluster, with b, the mean distance to the next nearest cluster: s = (b − a) / max(a, b). scikit-learn lists its drawback plainly: it's generally higher for convex clusters than for density-based clusters like DBSCAN's. In other words, silhouette and k-means share an idea of what a cluster is, so silhouette tends to reward k-means.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
customers = rng.uniform(size=(1000, 2))  # scaled spend and visits, no groups
for k in range(2, 7):
    labels = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0).fit_predict(customers)
    print(f"k={k}: silhouette {silhouette_score(customers, labels):.3f}")
# k=2: silhouette 0.360
# k=3: silhouette 0.380
# k=4: silhouette 0.413  <- "we found 4 customer segments"
# k=5: silhouette 0.382
# k=6: silhouette 0.379

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, silhouette_score

# Two crescents whose real groups we know, standing in for labeled examples
X, known = make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.05, random_state=0)
models = {"k-means": KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0),
          "DBSCAN": DBSCAN(eps=0.2)}  # a group = a dense, connected region
for name, model in models.items():
    labels = model.fit_predict(X)
    sil = silhouette_score(X, labels)
    match = adjusted_rand_score(known, labels)  # 1.0 = the same groups
    print(f"{name:<7} silhouette {sil:.3f}, match {match:.3f}")
# k-means silhouette 0.490, match 0.253
# DBSCAN  silhouette 0.335, match 1.000

content.text: On the noise, silhouette peaks at k=4 with 0.413, a number anyone could present as structure. On the crescents, k-means earns the higher silhouette, 0.490 against 0.335, yet its groups barely match the real crescents: an adjusted Rand index of 0.253, where random labels score close to 0 and identical groupings score 1.0. DBSCAN, whose definition of a group fits crescents, matches them exactly. The silhouette preferred the wrong answer, because it measures the k-means idea of a cluster, not the truth.
Your features decide the distances

k-means compares rows with Euclidean distance, so the columns you include, and their units, decide the groups. Leave income in dollars next to age in years and income alone draws the boundaries; that's why feature scaling matters for distance-based models. Add many weak columns and distances inflate, the curse of dimensionality: both scikit-learn and Google suggest reducing dimensions, for example with PCA, before k-means.
And the starting point
k-means always converges, but possibly to a local minimum that depends on the initial centers. scikit-learn uses k-means++ initialization by default and lets you run several starts with
n_init
. Google adds that outliers can drag centers or get a cluster of their own.

A wide group loses points to a tight neighbor
It returns k groups anyway, even from noise

Outliers drag centers or get their own cluster
The widest-ranging column draws the boundaries

blocks.title: Run the same pipeline on a null dataset

content.text: Shuffle each column independently, which keeps every column's distribution but destroys any joint structure, then run your exact pipeline on it. If your real data's silhouette isn't clearly above the shuffled data's, you have no evidence of groups yet.

After clustering, teams compare each group's average spend or age and call the differences insights. But k-means created the groups by splitting those very columns, so the averages are guaranteed to differ, even for clusters cut out of noise. A difference between clusters on the features you clustered on proves nothing.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Define a group before you cluster

content.text: Write down what the groups are for: customers who respond alike to a campaign, stores with similar demand. That decides the features, the distance and the algorithm.

items.title: Pick a method whose definition fits

content.text: Use k-means for compact, similar-sized groups,
GaussianMixture
for elliptical ones,
DBSCAN
for dense regions of any shape with outliers. Scale and select features deliberately.
Run the same pipeline on column-shuffled data. Structure that doesn't beat the null isn't structure.
Rerun with different seeds and on bootstrap samples, and compare the labelings with
adjusted_rand_score
. Groups that change on every run aren't a property of the data.
Check the groups against something the algorithm never saw: a labeled sample, or a downstream outcome, such as whether segments really respond differently to the campaign.
Key takeaways

items.text: Clustering always returns groups: on uniform noise, k-means "found" 4 with a silhouette of 0.413.
Each algorithm defines a group; k-means assumes round, convex groups with similar spread.
Internal scores share those assumptions: silhouette preferred k-means (0.490) over DBSCAN (0.335) on crescents that only DBSCAN recovered.
Decide what a group means for your decision, then test the clusters against a null, for stability, and against outside evidence.
